evidence: Plaut. Merc. 808: Syra. — Quis est quī mē vocat? — Erus atque alumnus tuos sum.
Plaut. Rud. 678: Obsecrō, quis est quī vocat?
terms.comment: In comedy, the question of someone who hears her name called and cannot yet see who is calling, which is just the case on the telephone. vocāre is also the verb of Traupman’s per tēlephōnum vocāre (see “call”).

evidence: Levi–Bini p. 283: Ades? — Adsum, quis mē vocat?
terms.comment: The short form, in a telephone conversation of 1937, where Ades? is the caller’s “Hello?” and Adsum the answer.

evidence: Ter. And. 267: quis hic loquitur? Mysis, salvē.
terms.comment: Said on hearing a voice before one knows whose it is.

phrases.latin: Syra. — Quis est quī mē vocat? — Erus atque alumnus tuos sum.
phrases.english: Syra! — Who’s that calling me? — Your young master, whom you nursed.

phrases.latin: Ades? — Adsum. Et tū quis? Nōnne Geōrgius, ut vōx sonat?
phrases.english: Hello? — Hello. And who’s this? Giorgio, by the sound of your voice?

phrases.latin: Quis est quī mē vocat? — Ego sum, avia tua.
phrases.english: Who’s calling? — It’s me, your granny.

phrases.latin: Tēlephōnum sonat. Quis vocat? Īnspice quadrum.
phrases.english: The phone’s ringing. Who’s calling? Look at the screen.

sources: Lewis & Short: voco · Lewis & Short: loquor
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), pp. 283, 285.
